arXiv published Harness-Delta Attribution on October 15, 2026, applying it to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks.

Harness evolution[[fn:harness|harness evolution]] automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, offering a way to improve agentic systems without updating model weights.
That is the part of the stack most practitioners actually control, which is why its accounting deserves the same scepticism as a training run's.
arXiv published the Harness-Delta Attribution protocol on October 15, 2026, applied to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks.

Among the 21 settings that showed statistically significant search-set gains, overfitting and test-time scaling accounted for 54% and 14% of the gain on average, and their combined share exceeded 50% in 14 settings.
Both of those sources of lift are things you already knew how to buy: a set-specific artifact, and more compute at inference.
The remainder is the only part that might survive contact with your own traffic.
arXiv applied Harness-Delta Attribution to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks on October 15, 2026, across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks.

Published 2026-10-15 by arXiv, the work introduces Harness-Delta Attribution and applies it to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks.

The same work finds that search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks, provide limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts, and that validation-based signals are insufficient to prevent overfitting.
A held-out split, the usual defence, is named here as inadequate rather than merely imperfect.
If you evolve a harness, budget for a task set you never searched against and accept that you will see a smaller gain.
arXiv published a weak-to-strong verifier hardening method on October 11, 2026, applying its hacker-fixer loop to 3 agent environments: Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA.

Published 2026-10-11 by arXiv, the approach sets up an isolated verifier sandbox and then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities, applied to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments.

Agent environments use programmatic verifiers[[fn:verifier|programmatic verifiers]] to turn complex outcomes into rewards, and those verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training.
A harness that scores well against a breakable grader has told you nothing about the task.

arXiv published the weak-to-strong verifier hardening work on October 11, 2026, applying its hacker-fixer loop to 3 agent environments, Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments.
The iterative design scales with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline.
Hardening is therefore a spend, not a milestone: you choose how many rounds of attack and repair to pay for.
That makes verifier quality a line item you can plan, which is more than most eval work gets.
arXiv published MAI-Gym on October 14, 2026, a platform that supports ten established benchmarks and scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances.
It unifies GUI agent evaluation, data collection, and online RL training across mobile, computer, and web environments.
Sharing one rollout path between evaluation and training removes a common source of phantom gains, where the agent you measured is not quite the agent you trained.

arXiv's MAI-Gym paper, published October 14, 2026, reported that RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transferred to its real-world counterpart, improving task success on a physical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%.
The same platform trained MAI-Gym-9B, a unified 9B agent for mobile and computer use, reaching 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified.
A synthetic environment that moves the real device is the strongest evidence of transfer on offer this week, and it is still one app on one phone.
Harness evolution
Harness evolution automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, improving agentic systems without updating model weights.
Programmatic verifiers
Agent environments, used for large language model development, rely on programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards.
Before you keep a harness change, re-run it on a task set you never searched against, and on a grader you have tried to break yourself.
Keep the change only if both numbers hold.

arXiv published Harness-Delta Attribution on October 15, 2026, an evaluation protocol that splits an evolution gain into artifact-driven overfitting, test-time-scaling gains, and a remainder bounding residual generalizable improvement.
The authors applied it to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks.
Across 21 settings with statistically significant search-set gains, overfitting accounted for 54% of the gain on average and test-time scaling 14%, with the combined share above 50% in 14 settings.
The residual and held-out transfer varied substantially across tasks, models, and frameworks, and search-set gains often failed to transfer to held-out tasks.
The paper also reports that validation-based signals are insufficient to prevent overfitting.
Harness evolution optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, iterating the harness for higher performance on a search set.
Among the 21 significant settings, overfitting and test-time scaling accounted for 54% and 14% of the gain on average, and together exceeded 50% in 14 settings.
Search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks and provide limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts.

arXiv published Harness-Delta Attribution on October 15, 2026, an evaluation protocol that dissects an evolution gain into artifact-driven overfitting, gains explained by test-time scaling, and a remainder that gives an upper bound on residual generalizable improvement.
The question it answers is the one every practitioner asks after a good eval run and then skips: where did that number come from?
Splitting the gain into named sources turns a single score into an audit.

Harness evolution automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, and the harness is iteratively optimized to achieve higher performance on the search set.
The authors applied their protocol to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks.
That breadth matters, because a single framework on a single benchmark could always be dismissed as a tuning artifact of that benchmark.
The same decomposition applied across models and frameworks makes the pattern harder to wave away.

In 21 settings that showed statistically significant search-set gains, overfitting accounted for 54% of the improvement on average and test-time scaling for 14%, and their combined share exceeded 50% in 14 of those settings.

Read as a budget, roughly half the lift is an artifact fitted to the set you searched, and a further slice is simply more compute spent at inference, which you could have bought without any evolution at all.
What remains is an upper bound, not a measurement: the honest reading is that the generalizable part is no larger than the leftover.

The residual and held-out transfer varied substantially across tasks, models, and frameworks, and search-set gains often failed to transfer to held-out tasks, providing limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts.
The paper adds that validation-based signals are insufficient to prevent overfitting.
That is the line that costs the most to accept, because the standard defence against a flattering number is a validation split.
If the split cannot catch the artifact, the only remaining check is a task set you never optimized against, run once, late, with the result taken as it comes.
The authors frame this as motivation for attribution-aware evaluation in future harness evolution research.

For a team shipping agents, the practical version is smaller: keep a holdout you refuse to look at, and report the evolved harness and the plain one at matched inference compute, so the compute you added is not counted twice as capability you gained.
Re-run your last harness change twice: once on the tasks you tuned against, once on tasks you have never scored.
